script.opening: "So the nurse said my iron’s sky high and you’d explain. I’ll be honest, I went straight online and now I’m worried I’ve got some sort of iron disease — and then I read it can be passed down, and that’s the bit that’s really getting me, because if I’ve got it, have I given it to my kids? My son’s 24. Have I done that to him without knowing?"

facts.text: If explored: tired for a couple of years, aching hands/knuckles (2nd/3rd MCP joints), reduced libido and erectile difficulties he’s been too embarrassed to raise, skin "tans easily even in a Welsh winter". All quietly attributed to "getting older / the job".

HIDDEN AGENDA — the guilt of inheritance. His real distress is not his own health but the fear he has passed a disease to his two children and that it’s "his fault". He half-knows his late father had "liver trouble" and "bronze" skin, never diagnosed, died at 60 — and now wonders if he ignored a clue he should have acted on.

If reached: father had diabetes, "went a funny colour", and heart failure; family always said it was the drink. Iwan now suspects it was this, undiagnosed — and is frightened of repeating it and of having handed it on.

~20 units/week he initially downplays; relevant because alcohol compounds iron-related liver injury — needs addressing without making the whole thing about drinking (which would echo the family’s wrong story about his dad).

Officially: an explanation of the iron result. Actually: to know whether he’s harmed his children, whether this is treatable, whether he’s repeating his father’s death — and reassurance that something can be done.

ice.ideas: He has "an iron disease" that is inherited and may already have damaged him and been passed to his kids.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt and fear about hereditary transmission to his two adult children ("have I done that to him?"), shadowed by a father who likely had the same undiagnosed condition and died at 60.
ice.expectations: An explanation and, underneath, reassurance that it’s treatable, that his children can be tested/protected, and that he isn’t simply repeating his father’s fate.

cues: "Have I given it to my kids?" — the consultation is about the family cascade and guilt as much as his own diagnosis.

Aching MCP joints + tanned skin + low libido + a raised HbA1c (47: non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, 42–47 per NICE PH38; diabetes is 48 or more) — the haemochromatosis constellation hiding in "getting older".
Alcohol downplayed and tied to the father’s story — handle without making it the whole narrative.

checkpoints.text: Explains the result clearly: very high ferritin with high transferrin saturation indicates iron overload, most likely hereditary haemochromatosis (genetic, often HFE) — and frames it as a common, treatable condition, not a cancer or a death sentence

Connects his "ageing" symptoms to the diagnosis: fatigue, MCP-joint arthralgia, skin pigmentation, reduced libido/ED, dysglycaemia (HbA1c 47: non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, not diabetes, needing monitoring — NICE PH38) — validating that these were the iron, not just age, and that treatment can help several of them

Addresses the central hidden agenda directly and accurately: it IS inherited (autosomal recessive HFE: if he is a C282Y homozygote each child carries at least one copy, and whether they are affected depends on their mother’s genes; his brother has a 1 in 4 chance of the same genotype), so first-degree relatives — his two children and his brother — should be offered HFE testing and iron studies (EASL 2022); but reframes guilt — he could not have known, it is no one’s fault, and CASCADE testing means any affected relative is caught early and protected

Explains treatment and prognosis honestly: regular venesection is effective, often normalises iron and improves symptoms/outcomes, and early treatment prevents the complications (cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy); arranges genetic confirmation and assessment of organ impact (EASL 2022: ferritin above 1000 µg/L with raised transaminases marks a higher risk of advanced fibrosis, so formal fibrosis assessment; liver imaging/specialist referral; venesection under a specialist to BSH 2018 targets)

Handles alcohol proportionately: advises minimising/avoiding alcohol because it compounds iron-related liver damage (his ~20 units a week is above the UK CMO 2016 low-risk limit of 14) — without reducing the whole diagnosis to drinking (which would repeat the family’s mislabelling of his father)
Recognises that the guilt about his children is the emotional core and responds to it first, rather than burying it in iron physiology
Gently explores and validates the father connection and the embarrassment-laden symptoms (libido/ED), making it safe to discuss

Safety-nets and plans: genetic test + organ-assessment results follow-up, referral as needed (hepatology/haematology), cascade testing for children and brother explained and supported, HCC surveillance (ultrasound every 6 months, NICE NG50) if cirrhosis is found, and a clear next-review — leaving him with hope and a concrete cascade plan

worked.txt: "Let’s take the scary word off the table first. Your body is storing too much iron, and the most likely reason is a condition called haemochromatosis. I know ‘disease’ and ‘genetic’ sound frightening, but here’s the headline: it’s common, it’s very treatable, and it is NOT cancer. People do well when it’s found — and yours has been found."

"And actually this might explain things you’ve been blaming on age: the achy knuckles, feeling wiped out, tanning easily, and — tell me if I’m right — maybe things being a bit flat in the bedroom? Those can all be the iron, not just getting older. Treating it can help with several of them."

"Now the thing that’s really frightening you — your kids. Yes, this runs in families, so your son, your daughter and your brother should all be offered a simple blood and gene test. But hear me on the guilt: you could not possibly have known, and this is nobody’s fault. The opposite of guilt is what we’re doing right now — because you’ve been diagnosed, we can check them EARLY, and anyone affected gets protected long before any harm. You haven’t handed them a fate; you’ve handed them a head start."

"You mentioned your dad — diabetes, a funny colour, heart trouble, blamed on the drink. It’s very possible he had exactly this, undiagnosed, in an era when nobody tested for it. That’s not you having missed something — and it’s precisely why catching it in you, and in your children, changes the story."

"The treatment is almost old-fashioned in how simple it is: we remove blood regularly — like donating — to bring the iron down, and it works. To confirm it we’ll do the gene test and check how your liver is doing. One honest thing: alcohol adds to the strain on an iron-loaded liver, so cutting right down really helps — that’s about protecting your liver, not a comment on your character or your dad’s."

"So: I’ll confirm the genetics, check your liver properly and likely involve a specialist for the venesection. I’ll give you the information to pass to your son, daughter and brother so they can get tested — and I’m happy to see them too. We’ll keep an eye on your liver long-term. You came in afraid you’d harmed your family. What’s actually happened is you’ve given them the chance to never get ill from this. That’s a good day, even if it doesn’t feel like it yet."

f.learning: A very high ferritin with high transferrin saturation is iron overload — most likely hereditary haemochromatosis — and the constellation often hides as "ageing": fatigue, MCP arthralgia, bronze skin, reduced libido/ED, dysglycaemia. It is common, treatable with venesection, and good outcomes follow early detection. The examinable core is the hidden agenda: the patient’s distress is not his own health but GUILT about hereditary transmission to his children, shadowed by a father who likely had it undiagnosed. Handle the genetics accurately (autosomal recessive HFE; first-degree relatives offered genetic + iron-study cascade testing) while actively reframing the guilt — he could not have known, and diagnosis means his relatives are caught early and protected. Address alcohol proportionately (it compounds liver injury) without reducing the diagnosis to drinking and repeating the family’s mislabelling, assess organ impact (formal fibrosis assessment, as ferritin is above 1000 with raised ALT — EASL 2022), note that HbA1c 47 is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia rather than diabetes (NICE PH38), and offer 6-monthly HCC ultrasound surveillance if cirrhosis is present (NICE NG50).

knowledge.guideline: British Society for Haematology haemochromatosis guideline (2018) · EASL haemochromatosis guidelines (2022) · NICE NG50 · NICE PH38 · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
knowledge.summary: A high ferritin with a high fasting transferrin saturation means iron overload; in a man of Welsh descent this is most likely HFE haemochromatosis. It is treatable with venesection, organ damage must be assessed, and first-degree relatives should be offered testing.

points.t: Ferritin rises with inflammation, alcohol, fatty liver and malignancy, so it is not specific. A raised fasting transferrin saturation shows true iron loading. A ferritin of 1180 with a saturation of 78% needs HFE genotyping; C282Y homozygosity is the commonest cause in people of northern European and Celtic descent (EASL 2022).

Fatigue, arthropathy of the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, skin pigmentation, low libido and erectile dysfunction, raised glucose and abnormal LFTs. These are often put down to age or alcohol for years. His HbA1c of 47 is in the non-diabetic hyperglycaemia range (42–47, NICE PH38), not diabetes, and needs monitoring.

EASL 2022: a ferritin above 1000 µg/L, especially with raised transaminases, marks a higher risk of advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis and needs formal fibrosis assessment. If cirrhosis is found, offer hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months (NICE NG50).

Regular venesection until iron stores are depleted, then maintenance, under a specialist to the ferritin and transferrin-saturation targets in BSH 2018. It improves fatigue and skin pigmentation and prevents progression; established cirrhosis and arthropathy may not fully reverse.

HFE haemochromatosis is autosomal recessive. If he is a C282Y homozygote, each child carries at least one copy; whether they are affected depends on their mother’s genes. A brother has a 1 in 4 chance of the same genotype. Offer first-degree relatives HFE testing and iron studies (EASL 2022).

Alcohol adds to iron-related liver injury: advise cutting right down, and stopping if fibrosis is significant. His 20 units a week is above the UK CMO 2016 low-risk limit of 14. Avoid iron and vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish.

Asked about jaundice, abdominal swelling, cardiac and diabetic symptoms; recognised ferritin above 1000 with raised ALT as a fibrosis risk.
Iron overload, most likely hereditary haemochromatosis, with the genetic test pending, in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

model.text: Hello Mr Pryce, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining. I know you’ve had the result and you’ve been reading about it. Before I explain anything, tell me what’s on your mind.
model.why: Invites his agenda before delivering information

model.text: Call me Iwan. The nurse said my iron’s sky high. I read it can be an iron disease that runs in families. That’s what’s getting me. My son’s 24. Have I given it to him without knowing?

That’s a big question and I promise we’ll answer it properly today. So I get it right for you, can I ask a little about how you’ve been, explain what the result means, then talk about your children? Does that work?
model.why: Commits to the key concern and sets a structure

model.text: Aye, fine.
The bloods were done for tiredness and aching joints. Tell me about those.
model.why: Open question on the presenting symptoms

model.text: Tired a couple of years. My knuckles ache, these two on each hand. I put it down to the building work and getting older.
Have you noticed any change in your skin colour?
model.why: Targets pigmentation from the haemochromatosis constellation

model.text: Funny you say that. I tan even in a Welsh winter. The wife jokes about it.
Too much iron can affect hormones as well. Some men notice a lower sex drive or difficulty with erections. Is that something that’s happened to you?
model.why: Normalises and asks directly about an embarrassing symptom

model.text: …Yes, to be honest. For a year or so. I haven’t said anything to anyone.
Thank you for telling me. It’s common, and it may well be part of this. Any thirst or passing more urine, breathlessness, swollen ankles or yellowing of the eyes?
model.why: Screens for diabetes, cardiac involvement and liver decompensation

model.text: No, none of that.
And roughly how much do you drink in a week?
model.why: Quantifies alcohol, which adds to liver injury

model.text: Not much. Few pints at the weekend. Maybe twenty units if I’m honest. Everyone said my dad’s problem was drink, so I watch it.
You mentioned your dad. Tell me what happened to him.
model.why: Follows the cue to the family story

model.text: Diabetes, heart failure, went a bronze sort of colour. Died at 60. Liver trouble, they said, from the drink. Now I’m wondering if it was this all along, and I never twigged.
That’s a lot to be sitting with: worry for your children, and wondering about your dad. What were you hoping I could tell you today?
model.why: Names both strands of guilt and elicits expectations

model.text: Whether it can be treated. Whether the kids are alright. Whether I’m going the same way as him.

Let me take those in turn. Your body is storing too much iron. The most likely reason is a condition called haemochromatosis, and the gene test we’ve sent will confirm it. It is common in people with Welsh and Celtic roots, it is not cancer, and it is very treatable.
model.why: Names the diagnosis, frames it accurately and defuses fear

model.text: Treatable how?

By taking blood off regularly, a bit like giving blood, until the iron comes down, then less often to keep it down. It often helps the tiredness and the skin, and it stops further damage. The joints and the bedroom side can improve too, though not always completely, and there are other treatments for those if needed.
model.why: Explains venesection honestly, including what may not reverse

model.text: And the kids?

It runs in families, so your son, your daughter and your brother should each be offered a simple blood and gene test. To be affected you need two copies of the gene, one from each parent, so your children’s risk depends on their mum’s genes too. And hear this: you couldn’t have known. Because it has been found in you, they can be checked early, before it ever harms them.
model.why: Accurate recessive inheritance, cascade testing, and reframes the guilt

model.text: So I’ve not doomed them.
No. You may well have protected them. And your dad could have had this at a time when nobody tested for it. That isn’t something you missed.
model.why: Addresses the father’s story without blame

model.text: Here’s the plan. I’ll chase the gene test and refer you to the liver team, because with your iron this high they’ll want a scan to see how your liver is coping. They’ll organise the blood removal. I’ll repeat your sugar test, because it’s on the high side of normal.
model.why: Specialist referral, fibrosis assessment and glucose monitoring

model.text: Right. That makes sense.
About drink: this isn’t your dad’s story being repeated. Iron and alcohol both put strain on the liver, so the less you drink, the better it copes. What would be realistic for you?
model.why: Alcohol advice that avoids echoing the family’s blame, and negotiates

model.text: I could stop in the week. Keep it to a couple at the weekend.

That’s a good start, and the liver team may advise more once they’ve seen the scan. Avoid iron or vitamin C tablets and raw shellfish too. I’ll give you a letter for your children and brother to take to their GP.
model.why: Practical advice and a concrete cascade tool

model.text: If you notice yellowing, a swollen tummy, vomiting blood, black stools, or new breathlessness or swollen ankles, ring us the same day. I’ll call you with the gene result, and I’ll see you again once you’ve met the specialist.
model.why: Specific red flags and a defined review

model.text: Okay.
When you speak to your son tonight, what will you tell him?
That I’ve likely got a treatable iron condition, it runs in families, and he should get a blood test from his GP with the letter. And that it’s nobody’s fault.
That’s exactly right. You came in thinking you’d harmed them. Today is the day you started protecting them.
model.why: Closes by reframing the emotional core

social.t: A builder with physical symptoms blamed on the job; two adult children and a brother who each need information. Offer a letter for relatives to take to their own GP.
The family blamed his father’s illness on drink. Handle alcohol advice so it protects his liver without repeating that stigma.

legal.t: His result is confidential. Relatives are informed through him, with his agreement, usually by a family letter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). He is an adult and his children are adults, so each decides about testing.

Under the UK Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, predictive genetic test results need not be disclosed for most policies (Huntington’s disease is the listed exception for large life cover). A diagnostic result, such as his, may need to be disclosed.

professional.t: Give honest information about what venesection can and cannot reverse, and let him choose his alcohol goal (GMC Decision making and consent 2020).
Coordinate the gene result, hepatology referral, HbA1c recheck and any HCC surveillance so nothing falls between services.

community.t: Haemochromatosis UK for patient and family information; some NHS Blood and Transplant centres accept people with haemochromatosis as donors during maintenance, per their eligibility rules.

redFlags: Jaundice, ascites, haematemesis or melaena: decompensated liver disease, urgent assessment
Breathlessness, oedema or palpitations: iron-related cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia
Ferritin above 1000 µg/L with raised ALT: higher risk of advanced fibrosis (EASL 2022)
psychosocial: Guilt about passing it to his children and brother
His father’s death at 60 and the family’s alcohol narrative
ice: Idea: “An iron disease that runs in families.”
Concern: “Have I done that to my son?” and repeating his father’s illness
Expectation: to hear it is treatable and that his children can be protected

playbook.diagnosis: Iron overload (ferritin 1180 µg/L, transferrin saturation 78%) with arthropathy, pigmentation, probable hypogonadism, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and mildly raised ALT: probable HFE haemochromatosis, genotype pending; fibrosis assessment needed.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body absorbs and stores more iron than it needs, and over the years it builds up in places like the liver, joints and hormone glands. It’s a common inherited condition, it isn’t cancer, and taking off blood regularly brings the iron down.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in afraid you’d harmed your children. Because we’ve found this in you, they can be tested early and never get ill from it.”
management.psychosocial: Family letter for his children and brother; handle alcohol without blame; invite a later appointment about erectile dysfunction if it persists after treatment.
sharedPlan: Chase HFE genotype; hepatology referral for fibrosis assessment and venesection to BSH 2018 targets
Cascade HFE testing and iron studies for first-degree relatives (EASL 2022)
Alcohol reduction he has chosen; avoid iron or vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish; repeat HbA1c
safetyNet: Same-day contact for jaundice, abdominal swelling, vomiting blood, black stools, breathlessness or ankle swelling
HCC surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound, with or without AFP, if cirrhosis is found (NICE NG50)

pitfalls.intro: This station is not failed on iron studies. It is failed by a candidate who explains the physiology and never answers the question he walked in with, or who turns it into an alcohol consultation that repeats the family’s mistake about his father.

items.fail: Launching into ferritin and transferrin physiology while his question about his son hangs unanswered.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The inheritance guilt is the emotional core.
items.fix: Acknowledge it in the first minute and promise to answer it; then answer it clearly before the end of minute 8.

items.fail: Telling him his children will definitely have it, or that they don’t need testing.
items.why: Inaccurate genetics. HFE haemochromatosis is autosomal recessive; first-degree relatives should be offered testing (EASL 2022).
items.fix: “You need two copies to be affected, so their risk depends on their mum’s genes too. A simple test will tell us.”

items.fail: Managing a ferritin of 1180 with venesection alone and no liver assessment.
items.why: Ferritin above 1000 with raised ALT marks a higher fibrosis risk; cirrhosis changes follow-up, including HCC surveillance (NICE NG50).
items.fix: Refer to hepatology for fibrosis assessment as part of the plan.

items.why: 47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NICE PH38); a diagnosis of diabetes needs 48 or more.
items.fix: “Your sugar is on the high side of normal; we’ll recheck it and it may improve as the iron comes down.”

items.fail: Making alcohol the headline: “this is why you need to stop drinking.”
items.why: It mirrors the family’s false story about his father and he disengages.
items.fix: Frame it as liver protection and negotiate a goal he chooses.

items.fail: Missing the erectile dysfunction because he never raises it.
items.why: Incomplete data gathering; hypogonadism is part of the picture and he is too embarrassed to volunteer it.
items.fix: Normalise and ask: “Some men notice a lower sex drive or difficulty with erections. Has that happened to you?”

Let me take those in turn. Your body is storing too much iron. The most likely reason is a condition called haemochromatosis, and the gene test we’ve sent will confirm it. It is common in people with Welsh and Celtic roots, it is not cancer, and it is very treatable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the diagnosis, frames it accurately and defuses fear

SCA_MODELS.text: Treatable how?

By taking blood off regularly, a bit like giving blood, until the iron comes down, then less often to keep it down. It often helps the tiredness and the skin, and it stops further damage. The joints and the bedroom side can improve too, though not always completely, and there are other treatments for those if needed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains venesection honestly, including what may not reverse

SCA_MODELS.text: And the kids?

It runs in families, so your son, your daughter and your brother should each be offered a simple blood and gene test. To be affected you need two copies of the gene, one from each parent, so your children’s risk depends on their mum’s genes too. And hear this: you couldn’t have known. Because it has been found in you, they can be checked early, before it ever harms them.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate recessive inheritance, cascade testing, and reframes the guilt

SCA_MODELS.text: So I’ve not doomed them.
No. You may well have protected them. And your dad could have had this at a time when nobody tested for it. That isn’t something you missed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the father’s story without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s the plan. I’ll chase the gene test and refer you to the liver team, because with your iron this high they’ll want a scan to see how your liver is coping. They’ll organise the blood removal. I’ll repeat your sugar test, because it’s on the high side of normal.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specialist referral, fibrosis assessment and glucose monitoring

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That makes sense.
About drink: this isn’t your dad’s story being repeated. Iron and alcohol both put strain on the liver, so the less you drink, the better it copes. What would be realistic for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Alcohol advice that avoids echoing the family’s blame, and negotiates

SCA_MODELS.text: I could stop in the week. Keep it to a couple at the weekend.

That’s a good start, and the liver team may advise more once they’ve seen the scan. Avoid iron or vitamin C tablets and raw shellfish too. I’ll give you a letter for your children and brother to take to their GP.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical advice and a concrete cascade tool

SCA_MODELS.text: If you notice yellowing, a swollen tummy, vomiting blood, black stools, or new breathlessness or swollen ankles, ring us the same day. I’ll call you with the gene result, and I’ll see you again once you’ve met the specialist.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red flags and a defined review

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
When you speak to your son tonight, what will you tell him?
That I’ve likely got a treatable iron condition, it runs in families, and he should get a blood test from his GP with the letter. And that it’s nobody’s fault.
That’s exactly right. You came in thinking you’d harmed them. Today is the day you started protecting them.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes by reframing the emotional core

SCA_STEM.name: Iwan Pryce
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods for fatigue and joint aches: ferritin 1180 µg/L, fasting transferrin saturation 78%, ALT mildly raised, HbA1c 47 mmol/mol, FBC and CRP normal. HFE genotype sent and pending. Alcohol recorded as about 20 units a week.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked by video to discuss “the iron result”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: British Society for Haematology haemochromatosis guideline (2018) · EASL haemochromatosis guidelines (2022) · NICE NG50 · NICE PH38 · UK CMO low-risk drinking guidelines (2016)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A high ferritin with a high fasting transferrin saturation means iron overload; in a man of Welsh descent this is most likely HFE haemochromatosis. It is treatable with venesection, organ damage must be assessed, and first-degree relatives should be offered testing.

points.t: Ferritin rises with inflammation, alcohol, fatty liver and malignancy, so it is not specific. A raised fasting transferrin saturation shows true iron loading. A ferritin of 1180 with a saturation of 78% needs HFE genotyping; C282Y homozygosity is the commonest cause in people of northern European and Celtic descent (EASL 2022).

Fatigue, arthropathy of the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, skin pigmentation, low libido and erectile dysfunction, raised glucose and abnormal LFTs. These are often put down to age or alcohol for years. His HbA1c of 47 is in the non-diabetic hyperglycaemia range (42–47, NICE PH38), not diabetes, and needs monitoring.

EASL 2022: a ferritin above 1000 µg/L, especially with raised transaminases, marks a higher risk of advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis and needs formal fibrosis assessment. If cirrhosis is found, offer hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months (NICE NG50).

Regular venesection until iron stores are depleted, then maintenance, under a specialist to the ferritin and transferrin-saturation targets in BSH 2018. It improves fatigue and skin pigmentation and prevents progression; established cirrhosis and arthropathy may not fully reverse.

HFE haemochromatosis is autosomal recessive. If he is a C282Y homozygote, each child carries at least one copy; whether they are affected depends on their mother’s genes. A brother has a 1 in 4 chance of the same genotype. Offer first-degree relatives HFE testing and iron studies (EASL 2022).

Alcohol adds to iron-related liver injury: advise cutting right down, and stopping if fibrosis is significant. His 20 units a week is above the UK CMO 2016 low-risk limit of 14. Avoid iron and vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; allowed the worry about his son to surface before any iron physiology.
Builder, family structure (two children, brother), the father’s death and the family’s alcohol narrative, his drinking.
Picked up “have I given it to him?”, the father’s ‘bronze’ skin and the embarrassment around libido, and explored each.
Idea (inherited iron disease), concern (guilt about the children, repeating his father), expectation (treatable, children protected).
HFE genotype; fibrosis assessment via hepatology; repeat HbA1c; ECG if any cardiac symptom; abdominal examination at a face-to-face visit.
HFE haemochromatosis vs reactive ferritin (alcohol, fatty liver, inflammation); transferrin saturation used to discriminate.
Asked about jaundice, abdominal swelling, cardiac and diabetic symptoms; recognised ferritin above 1000 with raised ALT as a fibrosis risk.
Iron overload, most likely hereditary haemochromatosis, with the genetic test pending, in plain words.
Hepatology referral for fibrosis assessment and venesection; cascade testing for children and brother; negotiated alcohol reduction.
Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia monitored; erectile dysfunction acknowledged with a plan; supplements and raw shellfish avoided.
Liver and cardiac red flags named; gene result phoned; review after specialist; HCC surveillance if cirrhosis found.

social.t: A builder with physical symptoms blamed on the job; two adult children and a brother who each need information. Offer a letter for relatives to take to their own GP.
The family blamed his father’s illness on drink. Handle alcohol advice so it protects his liver without repeating that stigma.

legal.t: His result is confidential. Relatives are informed through him, with his agreement, usually by a family letter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). He is an adult and his children are adults, so each decides about testing.

Under the UK Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, predictive genetic test results need not be disclosed for most policies (Huntington’s disease is the listed exception for large life cover). A diagnostic result, such as his, may need to be disclosed.

professional.t: Give honest information about what venesection can and cannot reverse, and let him choose his alcohol goal (GMC Decision making and consent 2020).
Coordinate the gene result, hepatology referral, HbA1c recheck and any HCC surveillance so nothing falls between services.

community.t: Haemochromatosis UK for patient and family information; some NHS Blood and Transplant centres accept people with haemochromatosis as donors during maintenance, per their eligibility rules.

redFlags: Jaundice, ascites, haematemesis or melaena: decompensated liver disease, urgent assessment
Breathlessness, oedema or palpitations: iron-related cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia
Ferritin above 1000 µg/L with raised ALT: higher risk of advanced fibrosis (EASL 2022)
psychosocial: Guilt about passing it to his children and brother
His father’s death at 60 and the family’s alcohol narrative
ice: Idea: “An iron disease that runs in families.”
Concern: “Have I done that to my son?” and repeating his father’s illness
Expectation: to hear it is treatable and that his children can be protected

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Iron overload (ferritin 1180 µg/L, transferrin saturation 78%) with arthropathy, pigmentation, probable hypogonadism, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and mildly raised ALT: probable HFE haemochromatosis, genotype pending; fibrosis assessment needed.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body absorbs and stores more iron than it needs, and over the years it builds up in places like the liver, joints and hormone glands. It’s a common inherited condition, it isn’t cancer, and taking off blood regularly brings the iron down.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in afraid you’d harmed your children. Because we’ve found this in you, they can be tested early and never get ill from it.”
management.psychosocial: Family letter for his children and brother; handle alcohol without blame; invite a later appointment about erectile dysfunction if it persists after treatment.
sharedPlan: Chase HFE genotype; hepatology referral for fibrosis assessment and venesection to BSH 2018 targets
Cascade HFE testing and iron studies for first-degree relatives (EASL 2022)
Alcohol reduction he has chosen; avoid iron or vitamin C supplements and raw shellfish; repeat HbA1c
safetyNet: Same-day contact for jaundice, abdominal swelling, vomiting blood, black stools, breathlessness or ankle swelling
HCC surveillance with 6-monthly ultrasound, with or without AFP, if cirrhosis is found (NICE NG50)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not failed on iron studies. It is failed by a candidate who explains the physiology and never answers the question he walked in with, or who turns it into an alcohol consultation that repeats the family’s mistake about his father.

items.fail: Launching into ferritin and transferrin physiology while his question about his son hangs unanswered.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The inheritance guilt is the emotional core.
items.fix: Acknowledge it in the first minute and promise to answer it; then answer it clearly before the end of minute 8.

items.fail: Telling him his children will definitely have it, or that they don’t need testing.
items.why: Inaccurate genetics. HFE haemochromatosis is autosomal recessive; first-degree relatives should be offered testing (EASL 2022).
items.fix: “You need two copies to be affected, so their risk depends on their mum’s genes too. A simple test will tell us.”

items.fail: Managing a ferritin of 1180 with venesection alone and no liver assessment.
items.why: Ferritin above 1000 with raised ALT marks a higher fibrosis risk; cirrhosis changes follow-up, including HCC surveillance (NICE NG50).
items.fix: Refer to hepatology for fibrosis assessment as part of the plan.

items.why: 47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NICE PH38); a diagnosis of diabetes needs 48 or more.
items.fix: “Your sugar is on the high side of normal; we’ll recheck it and it may improve as the iron comes down.”

items.fail: Making alcohol the headline: “this is why you need to stop drinking.”
items.why: It mirrors the family’s false story about his father and he disengages.
items.fix: Frame it as liver protection and negotiate a goal he chooses.

items.fail: Missing the erectile dysfunction because he never raises it.
items.why: Incomplete data gathering; hypogonadism is part of the picture and he is too embarrassed to volunteer it.
items.fix: Normalise and ask: “Some men notice a lower sex drive or difficulty with erections. Has that happened to you?”
